be.e: From Middle English been (“to be”). Further etymology of be and its conjugated forms The various forms have three separate origins, which were mixed together at various times in the history of English. The forms beginning with b- come from Old English bēon (“to be, become”), from Proto-Germanic *beuną (“to be, exist, come to be, become”).
A variant of by which goes back to Middle English be (variant of Middle English bi).
be.g: Alternative form of by. Also found in compounds, especially oaths, e.g. begorra begad and bejesus.

beach.e: From Middle English bache, bæcche (“bank, sandbank”), from Old English beċe (“beck, brook, stream”), from Proto-West Germanic *baki, from Proto-Germanic *bakiz (“brook”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“flowing water”).
beach.g: To run aground on a beach.

beacon.e: From Middle English beken, from Old English bēacn (“sign, signal”), from Proto-West Germanic *baukn, from Proto-Germanic *baukną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂u-, *bʰeh₂- (“to shine”).
beacon.g: A signal fire to notify of the approach of an enemy, or to give any notice, commonly of warning.

bead.e: From Middle English bede (“a prayer”), also “a bead for counting prayers” in a peire of bedes (literally “a pair of beads”), from Old English bedu, bed, ġebed (“a request, entreaty, prayer”), from Proto-West Germanic *bedu, *bed, *gabed, from Proto-Germanic *bedō, *bedą.
bead.g: Prayer, later especially with a rosary.

beak.e: From Middle English bec, borrowed from Anglo-Norman bec, Old French bec, from Latin beccus, from Gaulish *bekkos, from Proto-Celtic *bekkos (“beak, snout”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bak-, *baḱ- (“pointed stick, peg”). Dutch bek (“beak; bill; neb”).
beak.g: A rigid structure projecting from the front of a bird's face, used for pecking, grooming, foraging, carrying items, eating food, etc.

beak.e: Unknown; originally cant; first recorded in 17thC; probably related to obsolete cant beck "constable".
beak.g: A justice of the peace; a magistrate.

beam.e: From Middle English bem, beem, from Old English bēam (“tree, cross, gallows, column, pillar, wood, beam, splint, post, stock, rafter, piece of wood”), from Proto-West Germanic *baum, from Proto-Germanic *baumaz (“tree, beam, balk”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow, appear”).
beam.g: Any large piece of timber or iron long in proportion to its thickness, and prepared for use.

bean.e: From Middle English bene, from Old English bēan, from Proto-West Germanic *baunu, from Proto-Germanic *baunō (“bean”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”).
bean.g: Any plant of several genera of the taxonomic family Fabaceae that produces large edible seeds or edible seedpods.

bear.e: From Middle English bere, from Old English bera, from Proto-West Germanic *berō, from Proto-Germanic *berô (“bear”). On this theory, the Germanic languages replaced the older name of the bear, *h₂ŕ̥tḱos, with the epithet "brown one", presumably due to taboo avoidance; compare Russian медве́дь (medvédʹ, “bear”, literally “honey-eater”).
bear.g: A large, generally omnivorous mammal (a few species are purely carnivorous or herbivorous) of the family Ursidae; having shaggy fur, a very

bear.e: From Middle English beren (“carry, bring forth”), from Old English beran (“to carry, bear, bring”), from Proto-West Germanic *beran, from Proto-Germanic *beraną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti, from *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”).
bear.g: To carry or convey, literally or figuratively.

bearable.e: From Middle English berable, equivalent to bear + -able.
bearable.g: Able to be borne; tolerable; endurable.

beard.e: From Middle English berd, bard, bærd, from Old English beard, from Proto-West Germanic *bard, from Proto-Germanic *bardaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂, *bʰh₂erdʰeh₂.
beard.g: Facial hair on the chin, cheeks, jaw and neck.

bearded.e: From Middle English berded, either from Old English ġebearded or formed anew in Middle English; by surface analysis, beard + -ed.
bearded.g: Having a beard; involving a beard.

bearer.e: From Middle English berer, berere, from Old English berere (attested in Old English wæterberere (“waterbearer”)), equivalent to bear + -er.
bearer.g: One who, or that which, bears, sustains, or carries.

bearing.e: From Middle English beringe, berynge, berende, berande, berand, from Old English berende (“bearing; fruitful”) (also as synonym Old English bǣrende), from Proto-Germanic *berandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *beraną (“to bear; carry”), equivalent to bear + -ing.

beast.e: From Middle English beeste, beste, from Old French beste (French bête), from Latin bēstia (“animal, beast”); many cognates – see bēstia.

beat.e: From Middle English bet (simple past of beten "to beat"), from Old English bēot (simple past of bēatan "to beat"). Middle English bet would regularly yield *beet; the modern form is influenced by the present stem and the past participle beaten, perhaps by analogy with the Early Modern English paradigm eat:eat (“ate”):eaten.

beating.g: The action by which someone or something is beaten.

beautiful.e: From Middle English bewteful, beautefull (“attractive to the eye, beautiful”), equivalent to beauty + -ful. In this sense, largely displaced Old English fæġer (whence fair).
beautiful.g: Possessing beauty, impressing the eye; attractive.

beautify.e: From Middle English beutifien, from Old French beaute (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fine”), + -ify, from Latin facio (“make”).
beautify.g: To make beautiful; to increase the beauty of.

beauty.e: From Middle English bewty, bewte, beaute, bealte, from Anglo-Norman and Old French beauté (early Old French spelling biauté), from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fair”); see beau. In this sense, mostly displaced native Old English fæġernes, whence Modern English fairness.
beauty.g: The quality of being (especially visually) attractive, pleasing, fine or good-looking; comeliness.

because.e: From Middle English bi cause, from bi (“by”) + cause, modelled on Old French par cause.
because.g: By or for the cause that; on this account that; for the reason that.

beckon.e: From Middle English bekenen, beknen, becnen, beknien, from Old English bēacnian, bēcnian, bīecnan (“to signal; beckon”), from Proto-West Germanic *bauknōn, *bauknijan (“to signal”), from *baukn (“signal; beacon”).
beckon.g: To wave or nod to somebody with the intention to make the person come closer.

become.e: A compound of the sources of be- + come. From Middle English becomen, bicumen, from Old English becuman (“to come (to), approach, arrive, enter, meet with, fall in with; happen, befall; befit”), from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną (“to come around, come about, come across, come by”), equivalent to be- (“about, around”) + come.
become.g: begin to be; turn into (often with permanent states).

bed.e: From Middle English bed, bedde, from Old English bedd, from Proto-West Germanic *badi, from Proto-Germanic *badją (“resting-place, plot of ground”). If it is, the term is also cognate with Ancient Greek βοθυρος (bothuros, “pit”), Latin fossa (“ditch”), Latvian bedre (“hole”), Welsh bedd (“grave”), Breton bez (“grave”).
bed.g: A piece of furniture, usually flat and soft, on which to rest or sleep.

bedchamber.e: From Middle English bedchambre, bedchaumbre, equivalent to bed + chamber.

bedridden.e: From Middle English bedreden (also as bedrede), from Old English bedreda (“bedridden”, adj.), from bedreda, bedrida, bæddryda (“one who is bedridden”, noun), from bed, bedd (“bed”) + rida (“rider”), with -en by analogy with past participle adjectives.
bedridden.g: Confined to bed because of infirmity or illness.

bedroom.g: A room in a house, apartment, hotel, or other dwelling where a bed is kept for sleeping.

bedstead.e: From Middle English bedsted, bedstede, bedestede, from Old English bedstede (“bedstead”), equivalent to bed + stead.
bedstead.g: The framework that supports a bed; the rigid structural components of a bed, excluding the mattress, box spring, etc.

beer.e: From Middle English ber, bere, from Old English bēor (“beer”) (Oxford OED notes: "rare, except in poetry"), from Proto-West Germanic *beuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *beuzą (“beer”) (putatively from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewsóm), meaning “brewer's yeast”.
beer.g: An alcoholic drink fermented from starch material, commonly barley malt; often with hops or some other substance (like gruit) to impart a bi

beer.e: From Middle English beere, equivalent to be + -er.

beetle.e: From Middle English bitle, bityl, bytylle, from Old English bitula, bitela, bītel (“beetle”), from Proto-West Germanic *bitilō, *bītil, from Proto-Germanic *bitilô, *bītilaz (“that which tends to bite, biter, beetle”), equivalent to bite + -le.
beetle.g: Any of numerous species of insect in the order Coleoptera characterized by a pair of hard, shell-like front wings which cover and protect a

beetle.e: Borrowed from Portuguese bétele, from Malayalam വെറ്റില (veṟṟila) or Tamil வெற்றிலை (veṟṟilai).

befall.e: From Middle English bifallen, from Old English befeallan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifallan, from Proto-Germanic *bifallaną; equivalent to be- + fall.
befall.g: To fall upon; fall all over; overtake.

before.e: From Middle English before /bifore, from Old English beforan, from be- + foran (“before”), from fore, from Proto-Germanic *furai, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“front”).

beforehand.e: From Middle English biforhand, biforhond, beforehonde, bifornhand, equivalent to before + hand..
beforehand.g: At an earlier or preceding time.

befriend.e: From be- (intensifying prefix) + friend (verb). cognates Dutch bevrienden (“to befriend”) German befreunden (“to befriend”) German Low German befründen (“to befriend”) Saterland Frisian befrüündje (“to befriend”) West Frisian befreone (“befriended”)
befriend.g: To become a friend of (someone), to make friends with (someone).

beg.e: From Middle English beggen, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Old English *becgian, *bedcian, syncopated forms of bedecian (“to beg”), itself of obscure origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *bedukōn, a frequentative verb derived from Proto-West Germanic *bedu (“plea, petition, prayer”, whence English bead).
beg.g: To request the help of someone, often in the form of money.

beget.e: From Middle English begeten, from Old English beġietan (“to get”), from Proto-Germanic *bigetaną (“to find, seize”), equivalent to be- + get.
beget.g: To produce or bring forth (a child); to be a parent of; to father or sire.

beggar.e: From Middle English beggere, beggare, beggar (“beggar”), from Middle English beggen (“to beg”), equivalent to beg + -ar. Alternative etymology derives Middle English beggere, beggare, beggar from Old French begart, originally a member of the Beghards, a lay brotherhood of mendicants in the Low Countries.

beggarly.e: From beggar + -ly; adverb via Middle English beggarly, beggerly.
beggarly.g: In the manner of a beggar; poverty-stricken; mean; poor; contemptible.

begging.e: From Middle English beggin, beggyn, beggyng, (also beggand), present participle of beggen (“to beg”), equivalent to beg + -ing (participle ending).

begin.e: From Middle English beginnen, from Old English beginnan (“to begin”), from Proto-West Germanic *biginnan, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną (“to begin”), from be- + base verb *ginnaną also found in Old English onginnan.
begin.g: To start, to initiate or take the first step into something.

beginning.e: From Middle English begynnyng, bygynnynge, From Old English *beginnende (attested only as Old English onginnende), from Proto-Germanic *biginnandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *biginnaną (“to begin”), equivalent to begin + -ing.
beginning.g: Being the first portion of some extended thing.

begrudge.e: From Middle English bigrucchen (“to grumble at”), equivalent to be- (“at, about, over”) + grudge.
begrudge.g: To grudge about or over; be envious or covetous.

beguile.e: From Middle English begilen, begylen; equivalent to be- + guile.

behalf.e: From Middle English bihalve (“nearby”), from Old English bī healfe (“by side”), from bī (“by”) + healfe (“side, half”), equivalent to be- + half.
behalf.g: The interest, benefit, or wellbeing of someone or something.

behave.e: From Middle English behaven, bihabben (“to restrain, behave”), from Old English behabban (“to surround, embrace, hold, contain, hold back, withhold, restrain”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihabbjan, equivalent to be- + have.
behave.g: To conduct (oneself) well, or in a given way; to conform.

behavior.e: From Middle English behavoure, behaver, from behaven (modern behave), morphologically equivalent to behave + -ior. The suffix was adopted in imitation of havour (modern haviour, havior), an etymologically unrelated word that was corrupted from Anglo‐Norman Anglo-Norman aveir and Old French Old French avoir (“property, wealth”).
behavior.g: Human conduct relative to social norms.

behead.e: From Middle English beheden, bihefden, biheveden, from Old English behēafdian (“to behead”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihaubudōn, *bihaubidōn (“to behead”), equivalent to be- (“off, away”) + head.
behead.g: To deliberately remove the head of; to cut off (someone's) head.

behemoth.e: From Middle English behemoth, bemoth, from Late Latin behemoth, from Hebrew בְּהֵמוֹת (behemót). Most likely, the Hebrew word is an intensive plural of בְּהֵמָה (behemá, “beast”), from Proto-Semitic (compare Ge'ez ብህመ (bəhmä, “to be dumb, to be speechless”), Arabic ب ه م (b h m)).
behemoth.g: A great and mighty beast which God shows to Job in Job 40:15–24.

behind.e: From Middle English behinde, behinden, from Old English behindan (“on the back side of, behind”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihindan, *bihindini (“on the back side of, in the rear of, behind”), from Proto-West Germanic *bi- + *hindō (“the hind side, back part”), equivalent to be- + hind.
behind.g: At or to the back or far side of.

behold.e: From Middle English biholden, from Old English behealdan (“to hold, possess, preserve, belong, keep, observe, look at, take care, beware, be cautious, restrain, act, behave”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihaldan (“to hold with, keep”), equivalent to be- + hold.
behold.g: To look at or see (someone or something), especially appreciatively; to descry, to look upon.

behove.e: For the spelling with only one o representing /uː/, compare move and prove. The pronunciation with /oʊ/ is a spelling-pronunciation.

being.e: Originated 1250–1300 from Middle English being; see be + -ing.

beka.g: an ancient Biblical unit of weight, half a shekel

belch.e: From Middle English belchen, from Old English bielċan, from Proto-Germanic *balkijaną, *belkaną, probably ultimately of imitative origin.
belch.g: To expel (gas) from the stomach through the mouth; especially, to do so loudly.

belie.e: From Middle English belyen, beliggen, from Old English beliċġan, biliċġan (“to lie around, surround, hedge in, encompass”), from Proto-West Germanic *biliggjan, from Proto-Germanic *biligjaną (“to lie around”). Equivalent to be- (“around, by”) + lie (“to be positioned”).

From Middle English belyen, beleoȝen, from Old English belēogan (“to deceive by lying, be mistaken”), from Proto-West Germanic *bileugan (“to belie”). Equivalent to be- (“about”) + lie (“to deceive”).

belief.e: From Middle English bileve, from Old English lēafa, from Proto-West Germanic *laubu from Proto-Germanic *laubō. The replacement of final /v/ with /f/ is due to the analogy of noun-verb pairs with /f/ in the noun but /v/ in the verb, creating a pair belief : believe on the model of e.g. grief : grieve or proof : prove.
belief.g: Mental acceptance of a claim as true.

believe.e: From Middle English beleven, bileven, from Old English belīefan (“to believe”), from Proto-West Germanic *bilaubijan (“to believe”), equivalent to be- + leave (“to give leave or permission to, permit, allow, grant”). A related term in Old English was ġelīefan (“to be dear to; believe, trust”).
believe.g: To accept as true, particularly without absolute certainty (i.e., as opposed to knowing).

believer.e: From Middle English bilevar, bileever, belever, equivalent to believe + -er.
believer.g: A person who believes; especially regarding religion.

believing.e: From Middle English bilevyng, belevand, bileveand, belefand, from Old English *belēfende, ġelīfende, ġelȳfende. Equivalent to believe + -ing.

belittle.e: From be- + little. Coined by Thomas Jefferson in 1782.
belittle.g: To disparage, depreciate, or minimize the importance, value, merit, or significance of someone or something.

bell.e: From Middle English belle, from Old English belle, from Proto-West Germanic *bellā, from Proto-Germanic *bellǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-.
bell.g: A percussive instrument made of metal or other hard material, typically but not always in the shape of an inverted cup with a flared rim, wh

bell.e: From Middle English bellen, from Old English bellan (“to bellow; make a hollow noise; roar; bark; grunt”), from Proto-Germanic *bellaną (“to sound; roar; bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to sound; roar; bark”).

bellow.e: From Middle English belwen, from Old English belgan, bylgan (“to become angry, to swell with rage”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to sound, roar”), whence also belg (“leather bag”), bellan (“to roar”), blāwan (“to blow”). Potentially related to bawl, Swedish böl (“bawl”).
bellow.g: The deep roar of a large animal, or any similar loud noise.

bellows.e: From Middle English belwes, plural of belu, belwe, a northern form of beli, from Old English bæliġ, northern form of bielġ, from Proto-Germanic *balgiz. For the pronunciation /ˈbɛl.əs/, compare bodice, gallows.
bellows.g: A device for delivering pressurized air in a controlled quantity to a controlled location. At its most simple terms a bellows is a container

belly.e: From Middle English bely, beli, bali, below, belew, balyw, from Old English bielġ (“bag, pouch, bulge”), from Proto-West Germanic *balgi, *balgu, from Proto-Germanic *balgiz, *balguz (“skin, hide, bellows, bag”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell, blow up”).

belong.e: From Middle English belongen, bilongen, from Middle English be- + longen (“to be fitting, be suitable”), from Old English langian (“to pertain to, suit”), equivalent to be- + long (“to belong”).

belonging.e: From Middle English belonginge, belanging, belangand, equivalent to belong + -ing.

beloved.e: From Middle English beloved, biloved, equivalent to belove + -ed.

below.e: From Middle English bilooghe, equivalent to be- + low.

belt.e: From Middle English belt, from Old English belt (“belt, girdle”), from Proto-West Germanic *baltī̆, from Proto-Germanic *baltijaz (“girdle, belt”), from Latin balteus (“belt, sword-belt”), of Etruscan origin.
belt.g: A band worn around the waist to hold clothing to one's body (usually pants), hold weapons (such as a gun or sword), or serve as a decorative

bemoan.e: From Middle English bemenen, bimenen, from Old English bemǣnan (“to bemoan, bewail, lament”); equivalent to be- (“about, concerning”) + moan. Alteration of vowel from Middle to Modern English due to analogy with moan.

bench.e: From Middle English bench, benk, bynk, from Old English benċ (“bench”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg-.
bench.g: A long seat with or without a back, found for example in parks and schools.

bend.e: From Middle English benden, from Old English bendan (“to bind or bend (a bow), fetter, restrain”), from Proto-West Germanic *bandijan, from Proto-Germanic *bandijaną (“to bend”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to bind, tie”).
bend.g: To cause (something) to change its shape into a curve, by physical force, chemical action, or any other means.

beneath.e: From Middle English benethe, from Old English bineoþan (“beneath, under, below”), equivalent to be- + neath.

benefactor.e: From Middle English benefactor, borrowed from Medieval Latin benefactor (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin benefaciō (“benefit someone”), from bene (“good”) + faciō (“do, make”).
benefactor.g: Somebody who gives a gift, often money to a charity.

beneficial.e: From Late Latin beneficiālis (“beneficial”), from Latin beneficium (“benefit, favor, kindness”).
beneficial.g: Helpful or good to something or someone.

benefit.e: From Late Middle English benefytt, benefett, alteration (due to Latin bene-) of benfet, bienfet, bienfait (“good or noble deed”), from Anglo-Norman benfet (“well-done”), Middle French bienfait, from Old French bienfet, bienfait (“foredeal, favour”), from past participle of bienfaire (“to do good, do well”).
benefit.g: An advantage; help or aid from something.

benevolence.e: Circa 1400, original sense “good will, disposition to do good”, Old French benivolence from Latin benevolentia (also directly from Latin), literally “good will”, from bene (“well, good”) + volentia, form of volēns, form of volō (“to wish”), components cognate to English benefit and voluntary, more distantly will (via Proto-Indo-European).

bent.e: From Middle English bent-, preterite stem (as in bente, benten, etc.), and Middle English bent, ibent, ybent, past participle forms of Middle English benden (“to bend”). Equivalent to bend + -t.
bent.g: Folded or dented out of its usual shape.

bequeath.e: From Middle English biquethen, from Old English becweþan (“to say, to speak, to address, exhort, admonish, blame, bequeath, leave by will”).
bequeath.g: To give or leave by will; to give by testament.

bereave.e: From Middle English bireven, from Old English berēafian (“to bereave, deprive of, take away, seize, rob, despoil”), from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną, and Old English berēofan (“to bereave, deprive, rob of”); both equivalent to be- + reave.
bereave.g: To deprive by or as if by violence; to rob; to strip.

berry.e: From Middle English berie, from Old English berġe, from Proto-West Germanic *baʀi, from Proto-Germanic *bazją. The slang sense "police car" may come from the lights on the vehicles' roofs.
berry.g: A small succulent fruit, of any one of many varieties.

berry.e: From Middle English berȝe, berghe, from Old English beorġe, dative form of beorg (“mountain, hill, mound, barrow”), from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz (“mountain, hill”).

beryl.e: From Middle English beryl, from Old French beril, from Latin bērillus, bēryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”), in turn borrowed from Middle Indic forms like Pali veḷuriya or Prakrit 𑀯𑁂𑀭𑀼𑀮𑀺𑀅 (verulia), from Dravidian, probably named after Velur (modern day Belur) in southern India.
beryl.g: A mineral of pegmatite deposits, often used as a gemstone (molecular formula Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈).

beseech.e: From Middle English besechen, bisechen, prefixed form of Old English sēċan (“to seek or inquire about”); compare the doublet beseek, from the same dialect that gave seek. By surface analysis, be- + seech.
beseech.g: To beg or implore something of (a person).

beset.e: From Middle English besetten, bisetten (“to besiege, blockade; to fill, occupy; to harass, beset; to allot, bestow; to arrange, manage; to place, set; to provide for; to treat in a certain way”), from Old English besettan, bisettan (“to surround, beset; to set near; etc.”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisattjan.

beside.e: From Middle English beside, besiden, bisyde (also besides > besides), from Old English be sīdan, bī sīdan (“by the side (of), on the side (of)”). By surface analysis, be- + side.
beside.g: Next to; at the side of.

besides.e: From Middle English bisides (also bisiden), extension of biside, equivalent to beside + -s (adverbial suffix).

besiege.e: From Middle English besegen, bisegen, equivalent to be- (“around, about”) + siege.
besiege.g: To beset or surround with armed forces for the purpose of compelling to surrender, to lay siege to, beleaguer.

besom.e: From Middle English besme, beseme, from Old English besma, besema (“besom, broom, rod”), from Proto-West Germanic *besmō (“broom”).
besom.g: A broom made from a bundle of twigs tied onto a shaft.

best.e: From Middle English best, beste, from Old English bezt, betest, from Proto-Germanic *batistaz.
best.g: The supreme effort one can make, or has made.

bestead.e: From Middle English bistad; equivalent to be- + Old Norse staddr (“placed”), later assimilated to Etymology 1, above.

bestir.e: From Middle English bestyrien, bestirien, from Old English bestyrian (“to heap up, pile up”), equivalent to be- + stir.
bestir.g: To put into brisk or vigorous action; to move with life and vigor.

bestow.e: PIE word h₁épi The verb is derived from Middle English bestowen, bistouen, bistowen (“to give, bestow; to apply (something to something else); to arrange or have control over (something); to place (someone) in a position; to use (for some purpose); (reflexive) to find (oneself) a place to live or shelter”).
bestow.g: To apply or make use of (someone or something); to employ, to use.

beth.e: From Middle Bronze Age picture of a house by acrophony, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *bayt- (“house”).
beth.g: The second letter of the Phoenician alphabet, 𐤁

bethink.e: From Middle English bethenken, bithenchen (“to think about, consider”) from Old English beþenċan, biþenċan (“to think upon, remind, consider, remember”), from Proto-Germanic *biþankijaną; equivalent to be- + think.

betimes.e: From Middle English betymes, from bi (“by”) + time + adverbial -s. By surface analysis, betime + -s (adverbial suffix).
betimes.g: In good season or time; early, especially in the morning; seasonably.

betray.e: From Middle English betrayen, bitrayen (“to commit an act of treason against”), equivalent to be- + tray (“to betray”). Middle English bi- is from Old English be- (“be-”), from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”), from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near, by”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi (“at, near”).
betray.g: To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust; to give up treacherously or faithlessly.

betrayer.g: Someone who betrays, or reveals confidential information; a squealer or informer.

betraying.e: From Middle English betraying, bytrayenge, betraȝyng, equivalent to betray + -ing.

betroth.e: From Middle English bitrouthen, bitreuthen (“of a man: to pledge to marry; to give (a woman) in marriage, arrange the marriage of”), from bi- (prefix forming transitive verbs from nouns) + trouth, treuthe (“faithfulness, fidelity, specifically marital fidelity; promise, undertaking, specifically a promise of marriage; truth.
betroth.g: Of a man: to promise to take (a woman) as a future spouse; to plight one's troth to.

betrothed.e: From Middle English, equivalent to betroth + -ed.

better.e: From Middle English better, bettre, betre, from Old English betera (“better”), from Proto-West Germanic *batiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *batizô (“better”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰed-rós, from *bʰed- (“good”). False cognate of Persian بهتر (behtar).
better.g: An entity, usually animate, deemed superior to another; one who has a claim to precedence; a superior.

between.e: From Middle English betwene, from Old English betwēonum (“between, among”, dative plural, literally “by the two, near both”), from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”) + *twīhnaz (“two each”), corresponding to be- + twain. More distantly related to Ancient Greek διά (diá, “through, across, by, over”) whence English dia- (“through, across, between”).
between.g: In the position or interval that separates (two things), or intermediate in quantity or degree. (See Usage notes below.)

betwixt.e: From Middle English bitwixe, from Old English betweox, from Proto-Germanic *twiskaz (“twofold, double”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“twice, doubly; in two”). By surface analysis, be- (“by, near, around”) + twixt (“between”).

bevel.e: From Middle English *bevel, from Anglo-Norman *baivel (whence obsolete French beauveau) a diminutive of Old French baïf (“open-mouthed”), perhaps from baer (“to gape”), from Medieval Latin *batāre (“to gape, yawn, be open”), probably of imitative origin. If so, then related to Italian badare.
bevel.g: An edge that is canted, one that is not a 90-degree angle; a chamfer.

bewail.e: From Middle English bewailen, equivalent to be- (“over, about”) + wail.
bewail.g: To wail over; to feel or express deep sorrow for.

beware.e: From Middle English bewar, be war, be ware, forms of Middle English ben ware (“to be on one's guard, be vigilant”, literally “be ware”), equivalent to be + ware or be + aware.
beware.g: To use caution, pay attention to (used both with and without of).

bewilder.e: From be- (prefix used as an intensifier) + wilder (“to lead astray; to go astray, wander”).
bewilder.g: To confuse, disorientate, or puzzle someone, especially with many different choices.

bewitch.e: From Middle English bewicchen, bewycchen, biwicchen, equivalent to be- + witch.

bewray.e: From Middle English bewraien, bewreyen, biwreyen, from Old English *bewrēġan, from Proto-Germanic *biwrōgijaną (“to speak about; tell on; inform of”).
bewray.g: To accuse; malign; speak evil of.
To soil or befoul; to beray.

beyond.e: From Middle English biyonde, from Old English beġeondan, from be- + ġeond; related to yonder.
